displayQuote: Don't fight a battle if you don't gain anything by winning

meta.title: Who really said "Don't fight a battle if you don't gain anything by winning"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Patton through a 1979 memoir by his staff judge advocate, Porter B. Williamson. Later books credit Rommel. Wikiquote lists it as disputed.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Don't fight a battle if you don't gain anything by winning'?
meta.ogDescription: Not found in Patton's own writings. It traces to a 1979 memoir by one of his staff officers. A Rommel credit appears in 2009 and 2011 reference books.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Patton. The oldest printing found is Porter B. Williamson’s 1979 memoir I Remember General Patton’s Principles, which recalls it as one of Patton’s teachings. That is a staff officer’s memory, not Patton’s own words in any speech, letter or diary, and Wikiquote lists the line as disputed.

source.heading: Where the line comes from

docMeta.dd: Porter B. Williamson, Patton’s staff judge advocate, writing from memory
Tucson, Ariz.: Management and Systems Consultants, 1979; reissued as Patton’s Principles (Simon and Schuster, 1982)
“Never fight a battle when nothing is gained by winning”

source.excerpt: I remember Gen. Patton explaining, “So many battles are fought in war and in civilian life, …” […] “Don’t fight a battle if you don’t gain anything by winning.” Nothing would be gained by merely getting revenge against the enemy.
trail: 1979: Porter B. Williamson’s memoir I Remember General Patton’s Principles (Tucson) prints “Don’t fight a battle if you don’t gain anything by winning” in a chapter recalling Patton’s teaching (Internet Archive full-text result ↗).

1982: Simon and Schuster reissues the book as Patton’s Principles: A Handbook for Managers Who Mean It! with the same sentence (full-text result ↗). From there it spreads into quotation books such as William Safire and Leonard Safir’s Leadership (1990).
2009–2011: DK reference books credit the same words to Erwin Rommel’s Infanterie greift an (1937), for example World War II: The Definitive Visual Guide (full-text result ↗).
Today: Wikiquote lists the line under “Disputed” on both its Patton ↗ and Rommel ↗ pages and notes the conflicting citations.
source.excerptNote: Put together from Internet Archive full-text search snippets of the scanned 1979 book. The book is lend-only, so the full page could not be read and the gap marked […] has not been checked. The book shows the line in quotation marks in a chapter about Patton’s teaching. Williamson’s 1988 follow-up uses different wording: “…fight a battle if you do not gain anything when you win.”

source.rightsNote: The wording first appears in print in Williamson’s 1979 memoir I Remember General Patton’s Principles. That is a post-1931 work by a named author, so it is treated as in copyright in the U.S. No text written by Patton himself that contains this line has been found. A short quotation like this one is normally fine to use with attribution.

author.name: George S. Patton
author.heading: About George S. Patton
author.metaLine: 1885–1945 · U.S. Army general, commander of the Seventh and Third Armies in World War II
author.bio: George Smith Patton Jr. was a U.S. Army general who commanded the Seventh Army in the Mediterranean and then the Third Army in France and Germany during World War II. In 1942 he led the I Armored Corps and set up the Desert Training Center in California. Porter B. Williamson served on his staff there and later wrote down Patton’s sayings from memory.

misattribution.heading: Patton, Rommel, or a staff officer’s memory?
misattribution.intro: The same sentence is credited to two opposing World War II generals. Neither man is known to have written it down himself.

items.why: The Patton credit goes back to his former staff judge advocate, Porter B. Williamson, whose 1979 memoir recalls it as a Patton principle (1979 text ↗). It is a memory written down years after the fact. No speech, letter or diary entry by Patton has been found with this wording.

DK’s World War II visual history (2009) and Timelines of History (2011) credit the line to Rommel’s Infanterie greift an (1937). Wikiquote’s note gives page numbers in those DK books but none in Rommel’s own book (Wikiquote: Rommel ↗). The Rommel printings this check found are all far later than Williamson’s 1979 book.

items.who: “Never fight a battle if you don’t gain anything by winning”
items.why: Later quotation collections often start with “Never.” Williamson’s own 1988 book General Patton’s Principles for Life and Leadership words it as “…fight a battle if you do not gain anything when you win” (1988 text ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: the line comes from Porter B. Williamson’s 1979 memory of Patton’s teaching, not from anything Patton wrote. Wikiquote lists it as disputed ↗.

context.heading: Why the source matters
lead: Williamson’s books are collections of Patton’s teachings as Williamson remembered them, set down after Patton died in 1945. Williamson admits this himself. In another passage of the 1979 book he writes that the words he gives “are not exactly what Gen. Patton said,” because Patton used profanity.

That makes the Patton credit plausible and traceable to someone who worked closely with him. It still leaves the exact wording as Williamson’s, and it was through Williamson’s management-handbook reissue that the line reached business and self-help quotation books.
context.pull: These words are not exactly what Gen. Patton said.
